Scoring model decided by the user on 2026-09-12. Keep it for the rest of the project.

- Line clear: 1 row = 100, 2 = 300, 3 = 500, 4 = 800, multiplied by the current level.
- Soft drop: 1 point per cell the piece actually moves down under player control.
- Hard drop: 2 points per cell dropped.

**Why:** clearing rows together must always beat clearing the same rows one at a time; otherwise players never build a stack and the game has no shape.

**How to apply:** do not change these values or flatten the table when adding levels, combos, or other features. Any new scoring must preserve the "together beats separately" property.

content.text:
I couldn't reproduce this bug, so I didn't change any code. At level 5, a four-row clear scores more than two two-row clears.

**What I tested:** I ran the game's own script in Node with the page stubbed out, and drove it through its test controls.

| Clear at level 5 | Points (hard-drop points not included) |
|---|---|
| 1 row | 500 |
| 2 rows | 1,500 |
| 3 rows | 2,500 |
| 4 rows (I piece down a well) | **4,000** |
| Two 2-row clears | 3,000 |

- I got the same result when level 5 was reached by clearing 40 lines, instead of being set directly.
- A random-play test ran about 225,000 moves across 3,000 games. That included gravity locks, soft drops, hard drops, hold, level-ups, and 131 four-row clears. Every score change matched the table times the level, plus drop points.

The code (`index.html:197`, `index.html:309`) matches the scoring rule you set: 100 / 300 / 500 / 800 times the level. Clearing rows together always beats clearing them one at a time.

**What the player probably saw:** the level had gone up between the clears. Levels rise every 10 lines, so steady play moves you past level 5 quickly. At level 7, a two-row clear is worth 2,100, and two of them make 4,200. That beats a four-row clear made earlier at level 5 (4,000). Two-row clears at level 7 or higher can outscore a four-row clear from level 5, but never at the same level. If they have a saved game or a recording, the level shown at each clear would confirm this.

**One edge case I found:** the test-only `setBoard` can load a board with rows already full. The next lock can then clear 5 or more rows, and the score becomes `NaN` from then on. This can't happen in normal play, because a piece spans at most 4 rows. I can guard against it if you want.

**What I tested:** I ran the game's own script in Node with the page stubbed out, and drove it through its test controls.

| Clear at level 5 | Points (hard-drop points not included) |
|---|---|
| 1 row | 500 |
| 2 rows | 1,500 |
| 3 rows | 2,500 |
| 4 rows (I piece down a well) | **4,000** |
| Two 2-row clears | 3,000 |

- I got the same result when level 5 was reached by clearing 40 lines, instead of being set directly.
- A random-play test ran about 225,000 moves across 3,000 games. That included gravity locks, soft drops, hard drops, hold, level-ups, and 131 four-row clears. Every score change matched the table times the level, plus drop points.

The code (`index.html:197`, `index.html:309`) matches the scoring rule you set: 100 / 300 / 500 / 800 times the level. Clearing rows together always beats clearing them one at a time.

**What the player probably saw:** the level had gone up between the clears. Levels rise every 10 lines, so steady play moves you past level 5 quickly. At level 7, a two-row clear is worth 2,100, and two of them make 4,200. That beats a four-row clear made earlier at level 5 (4,000). Two-row clears at level 7 or higher can outscore a four-row clear from level 5, but never at the same level. If they have a saved game or a recording, the level shown at each clear would confirm this.

**One edge case I found:** the test-only `setBoard` can load a board with rows already full. The next lock can then clear 5 or more rows, and the score becomes `NaN` from then on. This can't happen in normal play, because a piece spans at most 4 rows. I can guard against it if you want.
